title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 18: Secretary of Justice v. Lantion and Jimenez: Due Process in Extradition Cases
keywords: Secretary of Justice v. Lantion and Jimenez
twin due process rights of notice and hearing
Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties
hold the oar of freedom in the stronger arm
primary_topics: Chapter 18 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's account of Secretary of Justice v. Lantion and Jimenez, in which the Supreme Court, by 9-6, first held that a prospective extraditee was entitled to notice and hearing during the executive department's preliminary evaluation of an extradition request, a ruling from which CJP dissented.

CJP's own Dissenting Opinion, which argued that the due process clause had no relevance because Mark Jimenez's 'life, liberty or property' was not in jeopardy during the evaluation stage, since no provisional arrest was sought, requested or even intended.

His two-phase framework for extradition -- a preliminary or evaluation stage that is executive and ministerial in character, and an extradition hearing that is judicial -- with the extraditee's full opportunity to be heard belonging to the second phase before the trial court.

The postscript: in a Resolution promulgated on October 17, 2000, the Court reversed itself by the same 9-6 margin, adopting essentially the arguments of the Puno and Panganiban dissents after Justices Quisumbing, Purisima and De Leon changed their votes.
sub_topics: The factual chronology: the November 13, 1994 RP-US Extradition Treaty, the US request of June 18, 1999 by Note Verbale No. 0522 for Mark Jimenez's extradition on five US Code charges, and the justice secretary's evaluation panel formed the same day.

Jimenez, through Counsel Estelito P. Mendoza, asked on July 1, 1999 for copies of the extradition request and time to comment; the request was denied, so he sued in the Manila RTC, where Judge Ralph C. Lantion ordered the officials to 'maintain the status quo.'
The precise question framed: during the evaluation stage undertaken by the executive department, was an extraditee entitled to the due process rights of notice and hearing?

The two phases of an extradition proceeding: the evaluation stage, an essentially executive determination of whether the request is properly supported, and the extradition hearing, a judicial process determining whether the person should be extradited.

The Melo ponencia's six reasons for the majority: the evaluation may lead to deprivation of liberty through provisional or temporary arrest; the procedure is 'akin to a preliminary investigation'; notice and hearing pervade administrative proceedings; the constitutional right to information applies; neither the Treaty nor PD 1069 precludes the twin rights; and the grant violates no norm of international law.
Justice Melo's closing call for freedom: the oar of freedom must be held 'in the stronger arm, lest an errant and wayward course be laid.'

CJP's first dissenting point: there was no danger of deprivation of liberty, because Article 9 of the Treaty requires urgency, a corresponding request, and that it be made before the extradition request -- none of which existed, and the justice secretary disclaimed any intention to seek provisional arrest.

CJP's second point: the evaluation stage is not adjudicative but executive and ministerial, merely the foreign affairs secretary's ascertainment that the Treaty's documentary requirements under Articles 3 and 7 are met, with the substantive issues reserved to the trial court.
CJP's third point: Jimenez's remedy for the alleged 'incalculable prejudice' was to fight the charges directly in the US courts, since only proof there could restore his reputation.

Justice Puno's separate Dissent: a historical review of extradition law from the Egyptians and Chinese through Grotius, Vattel, Kelsen, McDougall and Feliciano, proposing a 'balancing approach' and arguing that an extradition proceeding is sui generis, summary, without an accused, and that national interest deserves more deferential treatment than individual interest.

The postscript reversal of October 17, 2000, one week after CJP's printing deadline, with the Court adopting six grounds drawn largely from the erstwhile dissents, including the absence of any treaty or statutory grant of such rights, the Vienna Convention's good-faith reading, the weight owed the negotiating departments' interpretation, and the primacy of 'important state interests.'

stances.claim: A prospective extraditee is not entitled to notice and hearing during the preliminary evaluation stage, because his 'life, liberty or property' is not yet in jeopardy and the due process clause is therefore not engaged.
stances.rhetorical_move: narrowing the constitutional trigger to the actual factual milieu, then showing that none of the three requisites for provisional arrest under Article 9 of the Treaty existed

stances.claim: The evaluation stage is executive and ministerial, not adjudicative, so there was really nothing the extraditee could genuinely comment on at that point; his full opportunity to be heard comes before the trial court once an extradition petition is filed.
stances.rhetorical_move: two-phase institutional mapping that reassigns the due process opportunity to the later judicial phase

stances.claim: Jimenez's proper remedy against the reputational injury of the charges was to fight them directly in the US courts, not to attack the sufficiency of the supporting extradition documents here.
stances.rhetorical_move: remedy substitution: matching the alleged injury to the forum able to redress it

stances.claim: Justice Puno's separate Dissent held that extradition is sui generis and summary, that national interest is 'more equal than the others,' and that the denial of Jimenez's rights was 'too slight to warrant the interposition of judicial power.'
stances.rhetorical_move: reporting a colleague's international-law argument alongside his own constitutional one

notable_anecdotes: CJP recounts writing a separate Dissenting Opinion alongside Justice Puno against a 9-6 majority led by Justice Melo -- and then seeing the Court adopt their reasoning nine months later.
He notes that the trial judge who issued the status quo order, Ralph C. Lantion, had by the time of writing become a commissioner of the Commission on Elections.
He cites the transcript of the Oral Argument, where the secretary of justice stated that he had no intention of applying for the provisional arrest of Jimenez -- the factual pivot of the dissent.
He describes Justice Puno's 'scholarly Dissent' beginning with a history of extradition law running from the Egyptians and the Chinese to Grotius, Vattel, Kelsen, McDougall and Florentino Feliciano.
The postscript records that the reversal came on October 17, 2000, 'one week after my printing deadline' -- so the chapter reports its own overtaking by events.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 18 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' recounts Secretary of Justice v. Lantion and Jimenez, the extradition case in which the Supreme Court first held, by a vote of 9-6 in a forty-page Decision penned by Justice Jose A.R. Melo, that Mark Jimenez was entitled to copies of the extradition documents and an opportunity to comment even during the executive department's preliminary evaluation of the United States' request. CJP set out the chronology -- the November 13, 1994 RP-US Extradition Treaty, the US request of June 18, 1999 by Note Verbale No. 0522, the evaluation panel created that same day, Jimenez's denied request through counsel Estelito P. Mendoza, and the status quo order of Manila RTC Judge Ralph C. Lantion -- and then distinguished the two phases of an extradition proceeding: an evaluation stage that is essentially executive, and an extradition hearing that is judicial. He summarized the Melo majority's six reasons, including that the evaluation could lead to provisional or temporary arrest, that it was akin to a preliminary investigation, that notice and hearing pervade administrative proceedings, and that the constitutional right to information applied. He then reproduced his own Dissent: in the peculiar factual milieu of the case there was no danger that Jimenez would lose life, liberty or property, because Article 9 of the Treaty required urgency, a corresponding request, and priority to the extradition request, none of which was present, and the justice secretary had disclaimed any intent to seek provisional arrest; the evaluation stage was ministerial, confined to checking the Treaty's documentary requirements, so there was nothing the extraditee could genuinely comment on; and his remedy for reputational injury lay in fighting the charges in the US courts. He also summarized Justice Puno's scholarly dissent, which traced extradition law from antiquity to modern publicists, proposed a balancing approach, and held extradition sui generis rather than criminal. A postscript records that on October 17, 2000, one week after his printing deadline, the Court reversed itself by the same 9-6 margin, adopting essentially the two dissents' arguments after three justices changed their votes.
